source.text: Ὡς δὲ ἐγένετο ἀναχθῆναι ἡμᾶς ἀποσπασθέντας ἀπ’ αὐτῶν, εὐθυδρομήσαντες ἤλθομεν εἰς τὴν Κῶ, τῇ δὲ ἑξῆς εἰς τὴν Ῥόδον, κἀκεῖθεν εἰς Πάταρα·

records.literal_gloss: When now it happened [that] we set sail, having torn away from them, having run a straight course we came to Cos, and on the next [day] to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.

en.L: Now when it came about that we set sail, having torn ourselves away from them, we ran a straight course and came to Cos, and on the next [day] to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.
en.B: When we had parted from them, hard as it was, and put out to sea, we made a straight run to Cos. The next day we came to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.
en.R: It was hard to leave the leaders from Ephesus, but we said goodbye and got on the ship. We sailed straight to the island of Cos. The next day we sailed to the island of Rhodes. From there we went on to the city of Patara.

decisions.choice: we: the narrator counts himself among Paul's companions
alternatives: the narrator reports what others told him
decisions.reason: The "we" that began at 20:5 goes on here and runs to 21:18, as it did in 16:10-17. The writer includes himself in the journey. The text does not name him.

decisions.choice: having torn ourselves away: parting with difficulty
decisions.reason: The verb means to be drawn or pulled away. It follows the tears and embraces of 20:37-38: leaving the elders of Ephesus was hard.

decisions.choice: Cos and Rhodes: islands off the coast of the province of Asia; Patara: a port on the coast of Lycia
decisions.reason: Cos and Rhodes are islands in the Aegean Sea, each a day's sail apart. Patara was a harbor on the southern coast of what is now Turkey, a place to find a larger ship for the open sea.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "to Patara"
alternatives: some manuscripts read "to Patara and Myra"
decisions.reason: Some Western manuscripts, Codex Bezae among them, add Myra, a port further east where Paul later changes ships (27:5). Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the leaders from Ephesus; the island of; the city of
decisions.reason: Readable says who "them" were (the elders of 20:17) and what kind of places these were.

decisions.choice: parted from them, hard as it was
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the sense of a hard parting, as the meaning note explains.

source.text: καὶ εὑρόντες πλοῖον διαπερῶν εἰς Φοινίκην ἐπιβάντες ἀνήχθημεν.

records.literal_gloss: And having found a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, having gone on board we set sail.

en.L: And having found a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, we went on board and set sail.
en.B: There we found a ship bound across the sea for Phoenicia, so we went aboard and put out.
en.R: At Patara we found a ship that was going across the sea to Phoenicia. We got on it and sailed away.

decisions.choice: Phoenicia: the coastland north of Galilee, with the cities of Tyre and Sidon
decisions.reason: Phoenicia was part of the Roman province of Syria (21:3). Believers had gone there after Stephen's death (11:19), and Paul had passed through it before (15:3).

decisions.choice: crossing over: making the crossing over open sea
decisions.reason: The verb means to cross over. From Patara the ship sailed straight across the sea, as 21:3 shows.

decisions.choice: There; At Patara
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say where they found the ship, from 21:1.

source.text: ἀναφάναντες δὲ τὴν Κύπρον καὶ καταλιπόντες αὐτὴν εὐώνυμον ἐπλέομεν εἰς Συρίαν, καὶ κατήλθομεν εἰς Τύρον, ἐκεῖσε γὰρ τὸ πλοῖον ἦν ἀποφορτιζόμενον τὸν γόμον.

records.literal_gloss: Having sighted then Cyprus and having left it on the left, we were sailing to Syria and came down to Tyre; there for the ship was unloading the cargo.

en.L: And having sighted Cyprus and having left it on the left, we sailed on to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was unloading [its] cargo.
en.B: We came in sight of Cyprus and passed it by on our left, sailing on toward Syria, and we put in at Tyre, because the ship was to discharge its cargo there.
en.R: We saw the island of Cyprus, but we did not stop there. We passed to the south of it and sailed on to Syria. We stopped at the city of Tyre, because the ship had to unload the goods it was carrying.

decisions.choice: having sighted: coming in sight of land
decisions.reason: The verb means to make something appear. Sailors used it of land rising into view as they approached.

decisions.choice: leaving it on the left: they passed south of Cyprus on a straight course east
decisions.reason: Sailing east toward Syria with the island on their left, they kept south of it. The ship did not stop there.

decisions.choice: was unloading: the ship's business at Tyre was to unload its cargo
decisions.reason: The verb is a continuous form; it gives the reason for the stop, and the stay of seven days in 21:4 fits a ship being unloaded and reloaded.

decisions.choice: Tyre: an old port city of Phoenicia, in the Roman province of Syria
decisions.reason: Tyre lay on the coast north of Galilee. Jesus had been in its region (Luke 6:17, 10:13-14).

decisions.choice: we did not stop there; we passed to the south of it
alternatives: having left it on the left
decisions.reason: Readable says what "on the left" meant for a ship sailing east, as the meaning note explains.

source.text: ἀνευρόντες δὲ τοὺς μαθητὰς ἐπεμείναμεν αὐτοῦ ἡμέρας ἑπτά, οἵτινες τῷ Παύλῳ ἔλεγον διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος μὴ ἐπιβαίνειν εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα.

records.literal_gloss: Having sought out then the disciples, we remained there seven days; who to Paul kept saying through the Spirit not to go up to Jerusalem.

en.L: And having sought out the disciples, we remained there seven days. They kept telling Paul through the Spirit not to go up to Jerusalem.
en.B: We looked up the disciples there and stayed seven days. Speaking through the Spirit, they kept telling Paul not to go up to Jerusalem.
en.R: We found the followers of Jesus in Tyre and stayed with them for seven days. The Holy Spirit spoke to them, and they kept telling Paul not to go to Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: through the Spirit: the Spirit showed them what awaited Paul, and from that they urged him not to go
alternatives: the Spirit forbade Paul to go, and he went against the Spirit
decisions.reason: Paul says in 20:22-23 that he goes to Jerusalem bound by the Spirit, while the Spirit warns him in every city that chains await him. In 21:10-14 the pattern repeats: a prophecy, then friends pleading with him, then "the will of the Lord be done". So the warning came from the Spirit; the plea not to go was their own response to it. Paul is never blamed for going.

decisions.choice: kept telling: said it again and again
decisions.reason: The verb is in the imperfect, for something that went on during the seven days.

decisions.choice: the disciples: the believers at Tyre
decisions.reason: Believers had been in Phoenicia since 11:19. Paul's party had to seek them out in the city.

decisions.choice: The Holy Spirit spoke to them
decisions.reason: Readable says the Spirit spoke to them, which keeps open what the Spirit said, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: the followers of Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly who the disciples were, as at 6:2.

source.text: ὅτε δὲ ἐγένετο ἐξαρτίσαι ἡμᾶς τὰς ἡμέρας, ἐξελθόντες ἐπορευόμεθα προπεμπόντων ἡμᾶς πάντων σὺν γυναιξὶ καὶ τέκνοις ἕως ἔξω τῆς πόλεως, καὶ θέντες τὰ γόνατα ἐπὶ τὸν αἰγιαλὸν προσευξάμενοι ἀπησπασάμεθα ἀλλήλους, καὶ ἐνέβημεν εἰς τὸ πλοῖον, ἐκεῖνοι δὲ ὑπέστρεψαν εἰς τὰ ἴδια.

records.literal_gloss: When then it happened [that] we completed the days, having gone out we were journeying, accompanying us all with wives and children as far as outside the city; and having placed the knees on the shore, having prayed, \v 6 we said farewell to one another, and we went up into the ship, those then returned to the own [things].

en.L: But when it came about that we had completed the days, we went out and journeyed on, all of them accompanying us, with wives and children, as far as outside the city. And having knelt on the shore [and] prayed, \v 6 we said farewell to one another, and we went on board the ship, and those returned to their own [homes].
en.B: When our time there came to an end, we set out on our way again. The whole company, wives and children too, walked with us until we were outside the city. On the shore we went down on our knees and prayed, \v 6 and we took leave of one another. Then we boarded the ship, and they went back to their homes.
en.R: When the seven days were over, we left to go on with our trip. All the believers, with their wives and children, walked with us out of the city. We all knelt down on the beach and prayed. \v 6 Then we said goodbye to each other. We got on the ship, and they went back home.

decisions.choice: we completed the days: the seven days of 21:4 were over
decisions.reason: The verb means to finish or fit out. With "the days" it means that the stay had run its course.

decisions.choice: kneeling: praying on their knees
alternatives: standing, the more usual way to pray
decisions.reason: Jews often stood to pray (Luke 18:11, 18:13). Kneeling marks earnest prayer, as at the parting in Miletus (20:36) and in Jesus's prayer on the Mount of Olives (Luke 22:41).

decisions.choice: wives: the wives of the believers
decisions.reason: The word can mean women or wives. Set beside "children", it means whole families came out.

decisions.choice: their own: their own homes
decisions.reason: The phrase has no noun; "their own" means home, as in John 19:27.

decisions.choice: [homes]; homes; home
decisions.reason: English needs a noun here, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: All the believers
decisions.reason: Readable says who "all" were: the disciples of 21:4.

source.text: Ἡμεῖς δὲ τὸν πλοῦν διανύσαντες ἀπὸ Τύρου κατηντήσαμεν εἰς Πτολεμαΐδα, καὶ ἀσπασάμενοι τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς ἐμείναμεν ἡμέραν μίαν παρ’ αὐτοῖς.

records.literal_gloss: We then, the voyage having completed from Tyre, arrived at Ptolemais, and having greeted the brothers we stayed one day with them.

en.L: And we, having completed the voyage from Tyre, arrived at Ptolemais, and having greeted the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, we stayed one day with them.
en.B: We brought the voyage from Tyre to its end at Ptolemais, where we greeted the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} and spent a day with them.
en.R: We sailed from Tyre to the city of Ptolemais, and that was the end of our trip by sea. We greeted the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} there and stayed with them for one day.

decisions.choice: having completed the voyage: the sea journey ended at Ptolemais
alternatives: having continued the voyage from Tyre, with more sailing to Caesarea after
decisions.reason: The verb usually means to bring something to its end, so the voyage ended here and the party went on to Caesarea by land (21:8). Later Greek also used it for continuing a journey, and then they may have sailed on.

decisions.choice: Ptolemais: a port south of Tyre
decisions.reason: Ptolemais is the Old Testament city of Acco (Judges 1:31), on the coast south of Tyre and north of Caesarea.

decisions.choice: brothers: the believers there, men and women
decisions.reason: As elsewhere in Acts, the word means the members of the church.

decisions.choice: brothers and sisters, with "brothers" as the alternative
decisions.reason: The word takes in the whole church, as the meaning note explains.

source.text: τῇ δὲ ἐπαύριον ἐξελθόντες ἤλθομεν εἰς Καισάρειαν, καὶ εἰσελθόντες εἰς τὸν οἶκον Φιλίππου τοῦ εὐαγγελιστοῦ ὄντος ἐκ τῶν ἑπτὰ ἐμείναμεν παρ’ αὐτῷ.

records.literal_gloss: On the now next day having gone out we came to Caesarea, and having entered into the house of Philip the evangelist, being of the seven, we stayed with him.

en.L: And on the next day we went out and came to Caesarea, and having entered into the house of Philip the evangelist, who was [one] of the seven, we stayed with him.
en.B: The next day we left and came to Caesarea. We made our way to the house of Philip the evangelist, who had been one of the seven, and stayed as his guests.
en.R: The next day we left and went to the city of Caesarea. We stayed at the home of Philip. He was one of the seven men who had been chosen in Jerusalem to share out food to the widows. He was known as an evangelist, someone who told people the good news about Jesus.

decisions.choice: evangelist: one who proclaims the gospel
alternatives: a church office with set duties
decisions.reason: The noun comes from the verb for telling good news, which Luke uses of Philip in Samaria and on the road to Gaza (8:12, 8:35, 8:40). Compare Ephesians 4:11 and 2 Timothy 4:5.

decisions.choice: the seven: the seven men chosen in 6:3-6
alternatives: the seven deacons, as a later office
decisions.reason: Philip was named second among them (6:5). Luke never calls them deacons.

decisions.choice: Caesarea: the Roman capital of Judea on the coast, where Philip had settled
decisions.reason: Philip came to Caesarea at the end of 8:40, and is still there years later. Cornelius lived in the same city (10:1).

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "we came"
alternatives: many later manuscripts read "we who were with Paul came"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add "those around Paul", probably because a reading in church began at this verse. The sense is the same. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: chosen in Jerusalem to share out food to the widows; someone who told people the good news about Jesus
alternatives: the evangelist, one of the seven
decisions.reason: Readable says who the seven were (6:1-6) and what an evangelist was, as the meaning notes explain.

source.text: τούτῳ δὲ ἦσαν θυγατέρες τέσσαρες παρθένοι προφητεύουσαι.

records.literal_gloss: To this [man] now were daughters four, virgins, prophesying.

en.L: And this [man] had four daughters, virgins, who prophesied.
en.B: Philip had four daughters who were not married, and they prophesied.
en.R: Philip had four daughters. They were not married, and they spoke messages from God.

decisions.choice: virgins: unmarried young women
alternatives: women under a vow not to marry
decisions.reason: The word means a girl or woman who has not married. The text does not say whether they had chosen not to marry.

decisions.choice: prophesying: the gift promised in Joel and quoted by Peter
decisions.reason: Peter quoted Joel in 2:17-18: "your daughters will prophesy". Philip's daughters are an instance of it.

decisions.choice: who prophesied: it was their regular gift
alternatives: they prophesied to Paul on this visit
decisions.reason: The participle is present, describing them, not an event. Luke records no message from them; the warning to Paul comes from Agabus in 21:10-11.

decisions.choice: Philip
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the man.

decisions.choice: spoke messages from God
decisions.reason: Readable says what prophesying meant.

source.text: ἐπιμενόντων δὲ ἡμέρας πλείους κατῆλθέν τις ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰουδαίας προφήτης ὀνόματι Ἅγαβος, καὶ ἐλθὼν πρὸς ἡμᾶς καὶ ἄρας τὴν ζώνην τοῦ Παύλου δήσας ἑαυτοῦ τοὺς πόδας καὶ τὰς χεῖρας εἶπεν· Τάδε λέγει τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον Τὸν ἄνδρα οὗ ἐστιν ἡ ζώνη αὕτη, οὕτως δήσουσιν ἐν Ἰερουσαλὴμ οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι καὶ παραδώσουσιν εἰς χεῖρας ἐθνῶν.

records.literal_gloss: Remaining now [we] days many, came down a certain from Judea prophet named Agabus, \v 11 and having come to us and having taken the belt of Paul, having bound of himself the feet and the hands he said, Thus says the Spirit the Holy, The man of whom is the belt this, thus will bind in Jerusalem the Jews and will deliver [him] into hands of Gentiles.

en.L: And while we remained [there] many days, a certain prophet named Agabus came down from Judea, \v 11 and having come to us and having taken Paul's belt, [and] having bound his own feet and hands, he said, "Thus says the Holy Spirit: 'The man whose belt this is, the Jews in Jerusalem will bind in this way and will deliver [him] into [the] hands of [the] Gentiles.'"
en.B: During our stay of several days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. \v 11 He came to us, took Paul's belt, and bound his own feet and hands with it. He said, "Here is what the Holy Spirit says: 'Like this the Jews in Jerusalem will bind the man this belt belongs to, and they will give him up into the hands of the Gentiles.'"
en.R: We stayed there for several days. Then a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. \v 11 He came to us and took Paul's belt. He used it to tie up his own feet and hands. Then he said, "The Holy Spirit says this: 'The Jews in Jerusalem will tie up the man who owns this belt, just like this. Then they will hand him over to the Gentiles, the people who are not Jews.'"

decisions.choice: Agabus: the prophet from Jerusalem who foretold the famine in 11:28
alternatives: another man of the same name
decisions.reason: Luke introduces him as if new, but the name, the region and the gift are the same as in 11:27-28.

decisions.choice: from Judea: from the Jewish heartland around Jerusalem
alternatives: from the Roman province of Judea, which included Caesarea
decisions.reason: Caesarea was the seat of the Roman governor of Judea, yet Luke speaks of coming down from Judea to it. He uses Judea for the Jewish country around Jerusalem (1:8, 8:1).

decisions.choice: binding himself with the belt: a prophetic sign acted out, as the prophets of Israel did
decisions.reason: Prophets acted out their message: Ahijah tore his cloak (1 Kings 11:29-31), Isaiah went barefoot (Isaiah 20:2-4), Jeremiah used a linen belt (Jeremiah 13:1-11). The belt was a long cloth sash wound round the waist.

decisions.choice: Thus says the Holy Spirit: the prophets' opening, "Thus says the Lord"
alternatives: an ordinary way of reporting speech
decisions.reason: The prophets of Israel opened their messages with "Thus says the Lord", where the Hebrew has the divine name. Agabus puts the Holy Spirit in that place.

decisions.choice: the Jews will bind him and deliver him to the Gentiles: the outline of what happens, not every detail
decisions.reason: In 21:30-33 Jews seize Paul and the Roman tribune has him bound with chains. Paul later sums it up as being handed over from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans (28:17). The words echo what Jesus said of himself (Luke 9:44, 18:32).

decisions.choice: the Gentiles, the people who are not Jews
decisions.reason: Readable explains the word.

decisions.choice: Like this
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the force of the sign: Agabus points to the belt on his own hands and feet.

source.text: ὡς δὲ ἠκούσαμεν ταῦτα, παρεκαλοῦμεν ἡμεῖς τε καὶ οἱ ἐντόπιοι τοῦ μὴ ἀναβαίνειν αὐτὸν εἰς Ἰερουσαλήμ.

records.literal_gloss: When then we heard these things, were begging both we and the local [people] him not to go up to Jerusalem.

en.L: And when we heard these things, both we and the local [people] began begging him not to go up to Jerusalem.
en.B: At these words, we ourselves joined the people of the place in urging Paul again and again not to go up to Jerusalem.
en.R: When we heard this, all of us begged Paul not to go to Jerusalem. The people who lived in Caesarea begged him too.

decisions.choice: the local people: those who lived in Caesarea, the believers there
decisions.reason: The word means the people of the place. They are set beside "we", Paul's companions.

decisions.choice: we: the narrator himself joined the plea
decisions.reason: The pronoun "we" is stated for emphasis: even Paul's own companions, the writer among them, begged him not to go.

decisions.choice: were begging: they kept on pleading
decisions.reason: The verb is in the imperfect, for a plea that went on, as Paul's answer in 21:13 shows.

decisions.choice: Paul
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Paul.

source.text: τότε ἀπεκρίθη ὁ Παῦλος· Τί ποιεῖτε κλαίοντες καὶ συνθρύπτοντές μου τὴν καρδίαν;

records.literal_gloss: Then answered Paul, What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart?

en.L: Then Paul answered, "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart?
en.B: Paul replied, "What do you mean by weeping and crushing my heart?
en.R: But Paul answered, "Why are you crying? You are breaking my heart and making this hard for me.

decisions.choice: breaking my heart: crushing him with grief and wearing down his resolve
decisions.reason: The verb means to break in pieces. Their tears grieve Paul and also press him to give way; his next words show he will not.

decisions.choice: What are you doing: a gentle rebuke
decisions.reason: The question does not ask for an answer; it asks them to stop.

decisions.choice: making this hard for me
decisions.reason: Readable adds the sense of wearing down his resolve, as the meaning note explains.

source.text: ἐγὼ γὰρ οὐ μόνον δεθῆναι ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀποθανεῖν εἰς Ἰερουσαλὴμ ἑτοίμως ἔχω ὑπὲρ τοῦ ὀνόματος τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: I for not only to be bound but also to die at Jerusalem readiness have for the name of the Lord Jesus.

en.L: For I am ready not only to be bound but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus."
en.B: For my part, I am prepared to be bound in Jerusalem, and more than that, to die there, for the name of the Lord Jesus."
en.R: I am ready to be put in chains in Jerusalem. I am even ready to die there for the Lord Jesus."

decisions.choice: for the name of the Lord Jesus: for the sake of Jesus himself
alternatives: by the power of his name
decisions.reason: The name stands for the person, as when the apostles rejoiced to suffer for the name (5:41). The Lord told Ananias how much Paul must suffer for his name (9:16).

decisions.choice: I am ready: what Peter once said and could not keep
decisions.reason: In Luke 22:33 Peter told Jesus he was ready to go with him to prison and to death. Paul now says it on the way to Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: put in chains
decisions.reason: Readable says what being bound would mean for Paul.

source.text: μὴ πειθομένου δὲ αὐτοῦ ἡσυχάσαμεν εἰπόντες· Τοῦ κυρίου τὸ θέλημα γινέσθω.

records.literal_gloss: Not being persuaded then he, we were silent, having said, Of the Lord the will be done.

en.L: And since he would not be persuaded, we fell silent, having said, "The will of the Lord be done."
en.B: Since he would not be persuaded, we said no more except, "Let the Lord's will be done."
en.R: Paul would not change his mind. So we stopped trying to make him stay, and we said, "Let the Lord do what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} wants."

decisions.choice: the will of the Lord be done: words like Jesus's prayer before his death
alternatives: a common saying with no echo
decisions.reason: Jesus prayed on the Mount of Olives, "not my will but yours be done" (Luke 22:42), and taught his disciples to pray for God's will (Matthew 6:10).

decisions.choice: the Lord: the Lord Jesus
decisions.reason: Paul has just spoken of "the Lord Jesus" (21:13). But "the will of the Lord" can also mean God's will, and the difference is small here.

decisions.choice: we fell silent: they stopped pleading
decisions.reason: The verb means to be quiet. They gave up trying to persuade him, and said only the words that follow.

decisions.choice: we stopped trying to make him stay
decisions.reason: Readable says what their silence meant, as the meaning note explains.

source.text: Μετὰ δὲ τὰς ἡμέρας ταύτας ἐπισκευασάμενοι ἀνεβαίνομεν εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα·

records.literal_gloss: After now the days these, having made ready, we were going up to Jerusalem.

en.L: And after these days, having made preparations, we went up to Jerusalem.
en.B: After those days we got our things ready and set out on the road up to Jerusalem.
en.R: After that, we packed our things and started on the trip to Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: having made ready: getting baggage and animals ready for the road
decisions.reason: The verb is used of equipping for a journey: packing, and perhaps saddling animals.

decisions.choice: we were going up: the journey was under way
decisions.reason: The verb is in the imperfect; the arrival comes in 21:17.

decisions.choice: going up: Jerusalem stands high in the hills
decisions.reason: From the coast the road climbs to Jerusalem, and people always spoke of going up to it.

source.text: συνῆλθον δὲ καὶ τῶν μαθητῶν ἀπὸ Καισαρείας σὺν ἡμῖν, ἄγοντες παρ’ ᾧ ξενισθῶμεν Μνάσωνί τινι Κυπρίῳ, ἀρχαίῳ μαθητῇ.

records.literal_gloss: Went then also [some] of the disciples from Caesarea with us, bringing [us to one] with whom we would lodge, Mnason a certain Cypriot, an early disciple.

en.L: And [some] of the disciples from Caesarea also went with us, bringing [us to] Mnason, a certain Cypriot, an early disciple, with whom we were to lodge.
en.B: Some of the disciples from Caesarea came along with us. They took us to the house of Mnason, a man of Cyprus and a disciple from the early days, so that we could stay with him.
en.R: Some of the followers of Jesus from Caesarea went with us. They took us to stay at the home of a man named Mnason. He came from Cyprus, and he had been a follower of Jesus since the early days.

decisions.choice: bringing us to Mnason: they took the party to Mnason's house to lodge
alternatives: bringing Mnason with them from Caesarea
decisions.reason: The Greek is compressed: "bringing with whom we should lodge, Mnason". It most likely means they led Paul's party to Mnason. It could mean they brought Mnason along. The text does not say whether he lived in Jerusalem or at a stop on the way.

decisions.choice: an early disciple: a believer from the beginning
decisions.reason: The word means early or from the start, as in 15:7. Mnason may have believed in the first days of the church, perhaps at Pentecost (2:9-11).

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: they bring us to Mnason
alternatives: Codex Bezae reads that they brought us to those with whom we were to lodge, and on reaching a certain village we stayed with Mnason
decisions.reason: The Western text makes Mnason's home a stop on the two-day road from Caesarea. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the house of; the home of
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say where they were taken.

decisions.choice: followers of Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly who the disciples were, as at 6:2.

source.text: Γενομένων δὲ ἡμῶν εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα ἀσμένως ἀπεδέξαντο ἡμᾶς οἱ ἀδελφοί.

records.literal_gloss: Having arrived now we at Jerusalem, gladly received us the brothers.

en.L: And when we arrived at Jerusalem, the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} received us gladly.
en.B: When we came to Jerusalem, the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} were glad to welcome us.
en.R: When we got to Jerusalem, the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} there were happy to see us.

decisions.choice: the brothers: the believers in Jerusalem, men and women
decisions.reason: The elders meet Paul the next day (21:18). Here it is the believers who take the travelers in.

decisions.choice: arriving at Jerusalem: Paul came bringing the gift from the churches
alternatives: a visit with no stated purpose
decisions.reason: Paul later says he came bringing gifts for his nation (24:17), and his letters speak of a collection for the poor among the believers in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25-26; 1 Corinthians 16:1-4). Luke does not mention it here.

decisions.choice: brothers and sisters, with "brothers" as the alternative
decisions.reason: The word takes in the whole church, as the meaning note explains.

source.text: τῇ δὲ ἐπιούσῃ εἰσῄει ὁ Παῦλος σὺν ἡμῖν πρὸς Ἰάκωβον, πάντες τε παρεγένοντο οἱ πρεσβύτεροι.

records.literal_gloss: On the now following [day] went in Paul with us to James, all and arrived the elders.

en.L: And on the following [day] Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present.
en.B: On the day after, Paul took us with him to James, and the elders all came.
en.R: The next day Paul and the rest of us went to visit James. James was a leader of the believers in Jerusalem. All the elders of the church came too.

decisions.choice: James: the brother of the Lord, a leader of the church in Jerusalem
alternatives: James the apostle, the brother of John
decisions.reason: James the brother of John had been killed (12:2). This is the James of 12:17 and 15:13, whom Paul calls the Lord's brother (Galatians 1:19, 2:9).

decisions.choice: the elders: the leaders of the church in Jerusalem
alternatives: the elders of the Jewish people
decisions.reason: As in 11:30 and 15:2-6, these are the church's elders, who received gifts and met with the apostles.

decisions.choice: with us: the last "we" of this journey
decisions.reason: After this verse the writer does not speak of "we" again until the voyage to Rome (27:1).

decisions.choice: James was a leader of the believers in Jerusalem; of the church
decisions.reason: Readable says who James and the elders were, as the meaning notes explain.

source.text: καὶ ἀσπασάμενος αὐτοὺς ἐξηγεῖτο καθ’ ἓν ἕκαστον ὧν ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν διὰ τῆς διακονίας αὐτοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: And having greeted them, he began relating by one each [of the things] which did God among the Gentiles through the ministry of him.

en.L: And having greeted them, he related one by one each [of the things] that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry.
en.B: After greeting them, Paul told them, item by item, everything God had accomplished among the Gentiles through the service he had been given.
en.R: Paul greeted them. Then he told them everything God had done among the Gentiles while Paul was working among them. He told them about each thing, one at a time.

decisions.choice: what God had done: Paul tells it as God's work, not his own
decisions.reason: So Paul and Barnabas had reported before, telling what God had done with them (14:27, 15:4, 15:12).

decisions.choice: ministry: the service given to Paul
decisions.reason: Paul calls it the ministry he received from the Lord Jesus (20:24). The pronoun is Paul's.

decisions.choice: one by one each: a full, detailed account
decisions.reason: The phrase means item by item, leaving nothing out.

decisions.choice: the service he had been given
decisions.reason: Balanced makes clear that "his" is Paul, and that the service was given to him (20:24).

decisions.choice: while Paul was working among them
decisions.reason: Readable says what Paul's ministry was.

source.text: οἱ δὲ ἀκούσαντες ἐδόξαζον τὸν θεόν, εἶπόν τε αὐτῷ· Θεωρεῖς, ἀδελφέ, πόσαι μυριάδες εἰσὶν ἐν τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις τῶν πεπιστευκότων, καὶ πάντες ζηλωταὶ τοῦ νόμου ὑπάρχουσιν·

records.literal_gloss: Those then having heard were glorifying God. They said then to him, You see, brother, how many myriads there are among the Jews of those having believed, and all zealous ones of the law are.

en.L: And those who heard [it] glorified God, and they said to him, "You see, brother, how many tens of thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law.
en.B: On hearing this they glorified God, and they said to Paul, "Look, brother, at the tens of thousands of believers there are among the Jews, and every one of them is deeply devoted to the law.
en.R: When they heard this, they glorified God. Then they said to Paul, "Brother, you know that many thousands of Jews have believed in Jesus. All of them care very much about obeying the law of Moses.

decisions.choice: myriads: a very great number of believers
alternatives: exactly so many times ten thousand
decisions.reason: A myriad is ten thousand, and the plural was used for numbers too large to count (Luke 12:1). The number may include Jewish believers from abroad who had come for Pentecost (20:16).

decisions.choice: zealous: fervently devoted to the law
alternatives: members of the Zealot party who fought Rome
decisions.reason: The word means one who is eager or fervent for something. Paul uses it of himself before he believed (22:3; Galatians 1:14). Here it describes believers' devotion, not a political party.

decisions.choice: were glorifying God: they praised God for what they heard
decisions.reason: Paul had told what God had done (21:19), and the elders give God the glory.

decisions.choice: brother: Paul, as a fellow believer
decisions.reason: The elders call Paul brother; it is addressed to one man.

decisions.choice: deeply devoted to
decisions.reason: Balanced says what zeal for the law means, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: believed in Jesus; the law of Moses
decisions.reason: Readable says who they believed in and which law is meant.

source.text: κατηχήθησαν δὲ περὶ σοῦ ὅτι ἀποστασίαν διδάσκεις ἀπὸ Μωϋσέως τοὺς κατὰ τὰ ἔθνη πάντας Ἰουδαίους, λέγων μὴ περιτέμνειν αὐτοὺς τὰ τέκνα μηδὲ τοῖς ἔθεσιν περιπατεῖν.

records.literal_gloss: They have been informed now about you that apostasy you teach from Moses [to] those among the Gentiles all Jews, telling not to circumcise them the children nor in the customs to walk.

en.L: And they have been told about you that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles apostasy from Moses, telling them not to circumcise [their] children nor to walk in the customs.
en.B: Yet word has reached them that you are teaching the Jews scattered among the Gentiles to abandon Moses, and that you say they should no longer circumcise their children or follow the customs.
en.R: But they have heard reports about you. They have heard that you teach the Jews who live in other countries to stop obeying the law of Moses. People say you tell them not to circumcise their baby boys, and not to live the way Jews have always lived.

decisions.choice: they have been told: reports had been passed on to them
decisions.reason: The verb means to inform or instruct (Luke 1:4). It suggests the reports had been repeated until they were taken as fact.

decisions.choice: apostasy from Moses: forsaking the law given through Moses
decisions.reason: The noun means turning away or rebellion. "Moses" stands for the law he gave, as in 15:21.

decisions.choice: the charge: a report the elders do not accept
decisions.reason: In Acts Paul had Timothy circumcised (16:3) and kept a vow (18:18). His letters deny that circumcision makes anyone right with God (Galatians 5:6), yet tell a man who was circumcised when called to remain so (1 Corinthians 7:18-20). The elders call the report empty (21:24).

decisions.choice: walk in the customs: live by the Jewish way of life
decisions.reason: To walk is to live. The customs are the practices handed down from Moses (6:14, 15:1).

decisions.choice: their baby boys
decisions.reason: Readable says who was circumcised: boys, on the eighth day (Genesis 17:12; Luke 2:21).

decisions.choice: the Jews who live in other countries
alternatives: the Jews who are among the Gentiles
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly who these Jews were: those living outside the land of Israel.

source.text: τί οὖν ἐστιν;

records.literal_gloss: What then is it?

en.L: What then is it?
en.B: So what is to be done?
en.R: So what should we do?

decisions.choice: What then is it: what should be done about it
alternatives: what is the truth of it
decisions.reason: The short question asks what follows. Paul uses it the same way (1 Corinthians 14:15, 14:26).

decisions.choice: is to be done; should we do
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the question asks, as the meaning note explains.

source.text: πάντως ἀκούσονται ὅτι ἐλήλυθας.

records.literal_gloss: Certainly they will hear that you have come.

en.L: They will certainly hear that you have come.
en.B: There is no doubt they will hear that you have arrived.
en.R: They will surely find out that you are here.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "They will certainly hear"
alternatives: many manuscripts read "A crowd must certainly gather, for they will hear"
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add that a crowd must come together. Others, some of them early, lack it. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: they: the believing Jews zealous for the law
alternatives: the Jews of Jerusalem who did not believe
decisions.reason: The subject carries on from 21:20-21: the believers who had heard the reports.

source.text: τοῦτο οὖν ποίησον ὅ σοι λέγομεν· εἰσὶν ἡμῖν ἄνδρες τέσσαρες εὐχὴν ἔχοντες ἀφ’ ἑαυτῶν.

records.literal_gloss: This therefore do, what to you we say. There are with us men four a vow having upon themselves.

en.L: So do this, which we tell you: there are with us four men who have a vow on themselves.
en.B: Here is our advice, then. Four men among us have taken a vow on themselves.
en.R: So please do what we say. Four men in our group have made a special promise to God.

decisions.choice: a vow: most likely a Nazirite vow
alternatives: a private promise of some other kind
decisions.reason: The text does not name the vow. The shaving of the head and the offerings in 21:24-26 fit the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6:1-21, which ended with shaving the head at the sanctuary (Numbers 6:18). Paul had kept a vow of his own (18:18).

decisions.choice: with us: from among the believers
decisions.reason: The pronoun places the four men among the church in Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: having a vow on themselves: they had taken the vow on themselves
alternatives: a vow laid on them by others
decisions.reason: A Nazirite vow was taken freely (Numbers 6:2).

decisions.choice: a special promise to God
decisions.reason: Readable says what a vow is.

source.text: τούτους παραλαβὼν ἁγνίσθητι σὺν αὐτοῖς καὶ δαπάνησον ἐπ’ αὐτοῖς ἵνα ξυρήσονται τὴν κεφαλήν, καὶ γνώσονται πάντες ὅτι ὧν κατήχηνται περὶ σοῦ οὐδέν ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ στοιχεῖς καὶ αὐτὸς φυλάσσων τὸν νόμον.

records.literal_gloss: These having taken, be purified with them and pay expenses for them, so that they will shave the head, and will know all that [of the things] of which they have been informed about you nothing is, but you walk orderly also yourself keeping the law.

en.L: Take these [men], be purified with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave [their] heads, and all will know that there is nothing in the things they have been told about you, but that you yourself also walk in order, keeping the law.
en.B: Bring these men with you, be purified along with them, and cover the cost of their offerings so that they can shave their heads. Then everyone will see that the reports about you are empty, and that you yourself live in line with the law and keep it.
en.R: Take these men with you. Go through the ceremony that makes you clean, together with them. Pay for the sacrifices they must offer, so that they can shave their heads. Then everyone will know that what they heard about you is not true. They will see that you also obey the law of Moses.

decisions.choice: pay their expenses: pay for the offerings that ended the vow
alternatives: pay for their food and lodging
decisions.reason: At the end of a Nazirite vow a man offered a male lamb, a ewe lamb and a ram, with grain and drink offerings (Numbers 6:14-15), which was costly for four men. Paying for others' offerings was counted an act of devotion; Josephus says King Agrippa I paid for many Nazirites to shave their heads (Antiquities 19.294).

decisions.choice: be purified with them: Paul's own ritual cleansing, alongside the four men
alternatives: Paul takes the Nazirite vow himself
decisions.reason: The text does not say why Paul needed cleansing. A Jew returning from Gentile lands could be treated as unclean and was cleansed over seven days, on the third and the seventh (Numbers 19:12); 21:27 speaks of seven days. A Nazirite vow usually lasted longer than a week.

decisions.choice: you walk in order: you live in line with the law
decisions.reason: The verb means to keep in line or in step. Paul uses it for living by a rule (Galatians 5:25, 6:16; Philippians 3:16).

decisions.choice: shave the head: each man shaves his own head
decisions.reason: The noun is singular, for the head of each man.

decisions.choice: the cost of their offerings
decisions.reason: Balanced says what the expenses were, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: the ceremony that makes you clean; pay for the sacrifices they must offer
decisions.reason: Readable says what purification and the expenses were.

source.text: περὶ δὲ τῶν πεπιστευκότων ἐθνῶν ἡμεῖς ἀπεστείλαμεν κρίναντες φυλάσσεσθαι αὐτοὺς τό τε εἰδωλόθυτον καὶ αἷμα καὶ πνικτὸν καὶ πορνείαν.

records.literal_gloss: Concerning now the having believed Gentiles, we sent, having judged [that] to keep themselves them from both the [thing] sacrificed to idols and blood and strangled and sexual immorality.

en.L: But concerning the Gentiles who have believed, we sent [word], having judged that they should keep themselves from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what is strangled, and from sexual immorality."
en.B: For the Gentiles who have come to believe, we have already written what we decided: they are to avoid meat sacrificed to idols, and blood, and anything strangled, and sexual immorality."
en.R: As for the Gentiles who have believed, we already sent them a letter. We told them what we had decided. They must not eat meat that was offered to idols. They must not eat blood, or meat from animals that were strangled. And they must not commit sexual sins."

decisions.choice: the letter sent after the meeting in Jerusalem (15:20, 15:23-29)
decisions.reason: The four things are those James named in 15:20 and the letter set down in 15:29. The elders recall it to make clear that what they ask of Paul concerns Jews; nothing more is asked of Gentile believers.

decisions.choice: strangled: meat from animals killed without draining the blood
decisions.reason: The law told Israel to pour out the blood of an animal killed for food (Leviticus 17:13-14). An animal strangled still had its blood in it.

decisions.choice: sexual immorality: sexual relations outside marriage, including unions the law forbids
decisions.reason: The word covers every kind of sexual sin. Set beside the food laws, it likely includes the forbidden unions of Leviticus 18.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "having judged that they should keep themselves from"
alternatives: many later manuscripts read "having judged that they observe no such thing, except that they keep themselves from"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add a phrase saying Gentiles need keep none of these customs except the four things. It states what the shorter text implies. Codex Bezae also leaves out "strangled", as it does in 15:20 and 15:29. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: sent them a letter
decisions.reason: Readable says what was sent: the letter of 15:23-29.

decisions.choice: commit sexual sins
decisions.reason: Readable uses plainer words, as the meaning note explains.

source.text: τότε ὁ Παῦλος παραλαβὼν τοὺς ἄνδρας τῇ ἐχομένῃ ἡμέρᾳ σὺν αὐτοῖς ἁγνισθεὶς εἰσῄει εἰς τὸ ἱερόν, διαγγέλλων τὴν ἐκπλήρωσιν τῶν ἡμερῶν τοῦ ἁγνισμοῦ ἕως οὗ προσηνέχθη ὑπὲρ ἑνὸς ἑκάστου αὐτῶν ἡ προσφορά.

records.literal_gloss: Then Paul having taken the men, on the following day with them having been purified, entered into the temple, declaring the completion of the days of the purification, until which was offered for one each of them the offering.

en.L: Then Paul took the men, and on the following day, having been purified with them, he entered into the temple, giving notice of the completion of the days of purification, until the offering was offered for each one of them.
en.B: Then Paul took the men along. On the following day he was purified with them and went into the temple, announcing when their days of purification would be over and the offering for each of them would be presented.
en.R: So Paul took the four men with him. The next day he went through the ceremony to make himself clean, along with them. Then he went into the temple. He told the priests when their time of being made clean would be finished. Then a sacrifice would be offered for each of the men.

decisions.choice: giving notice: announcing the day when the purification would end and the offerings would be made
alternatives: Paul kept going to the temple until the offerings were made
decisions.reason: The phrase "until the offering was offered" most likely tells what the notice was about: the time up to the offering. It could also mean Paul kept attending the temple until that day.

decisions.choice: giving notice: to the priests, who would prepare to receive the offerings
decisions.reason: The text does not name the hearers. Offerings were brought to the priests at the temple (Numbers 6:16-17).

decisions.choice: having been purified: Paul's own cleansing began
decisions.reason: In 21:27 the seven days are still not over, so the cleansing began that day and was still under way.

decisions.choice: He told the priests
decisions.reason: Readable names who heard the notice, as the meaning note explains.

source.text: Ὡς δὲ ἔμελλον αἱ ἑπτὰ ἡμέραι συντελεῖσθαι, οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀσίας Ἰουδαῖοι θεασάμενοι αὐτὸν ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ συνέχεον πάντα τὸν ὄχλον καὶ ἐπέβαλον ἐπ’ αὐτὸν τὰς χεῖρας, κράζοντες· Ἄνδρες Ἰσραηλῖται, βοηθεῖτε· οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὁ κατὰ τοῦ λαοῦ καὶ τοῦ νόμου καὶ τοῦ τόπου τούτου πάντας πανταχῇ διδάσκων, ἔτι τε καὶ Ἕλληνας εἰσήγαγεν εἰς τὸ ἱερὸν καὶ κεκοίνωκεν τὸν ἅγιον τόπον τοῦτον.

records.literal_gloss: When now were about the seven days to be completed, the from Asia Jews, having seen him in the temple, were stirring up all the crowd and laid upon him the hands, \v 28 crying out, Men, Israelites, help! This is the man who against the people and the law and the place this all [people] everywhere [is] teaching; besides also Greeks he brought into the temple and has defiled the holy place this.

en.L: And when the seven days were about to be completed, the Jews from Asia, having seen him in the temple, stirred up all the crowd and laid hands on him, \v 28 crying out, "Men, Israelites, help! This is the man who teaches all [people] everywhere against the people and the law and this place, and besides, he has even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place."
en.B: The seven days were nearly over when some Jews from Asia caught sight of Paul in the temple. They threw the whole crowd into confusion and laid hands on him, \v 28 shouting, "{{gender:People|Men}} of Israel, help! This is the man whose teaching, everywhere he goes, sets everyone against our people, the law and this place. And now he has even brought Greeks into the temple and made this holy place unclean."
en.R: The seven days were almost finished. Then some Jews from the province of Asia saw Paul in the temple. They got the whole crowd excited, and they grabbed Paul. \v 28 They shouted, "People of Israel, help us! This man goes everywhere teaching everyone things against our people, against God's law, and against this temple. And now he has brought Greeks into the temple, and he has made this holy place unclean!"

decisions.choice: the seven days: the days of purification of 21:24-26
alternatives: the seven days of the feast of Pentecost
decisions.reason: Cleansing took seven days (Numbers 19:12). Paul had been purified and was keeping those days in the temple.

decisions.choice: the Jews from Asia: Jews from the province of Asia, in Jerusalem for the feast
decisions.reason: Asia was the Roman province whose chief city was Ephesus, where Jews had opposed Paul (19:9; 20:19). Paul hurried to Jerusalem for Pentecost (20:16). They knew Trophimus by sight (21:29).

decisions.choice: men, Israelites: a call to the people of Israel
alternatives: a call to the men only
decisions.reason: It is the formal way of addressing the people, as at 2:22 and 3:12. The cry goes to the whole crowd, though in the inner courts it may have been mostly men.

decisions.choice: bringing Greeks into the temple: taking Gentiles past the barrier into the inner courts
alternatives: bringing them into the outer court, which was open to all
decisions.reason: Gentiles could enter the outer court, but a low wall barred them from the courts beyond. Josephus describes notices on it in Greek and Latin forbidding foreigners to enter (Jewish War 5.193-194), and one of these warning inscriptions, threatening death, has been found.

decisions.choice: against the people, the law and this place: the charge once made against Stephen
decisions.reason: False witnesses said Stephen spoke against this holy place and the law (6:13-14).

decisions.choice: has defiled: made common, made unclean
decisions.reason: The verb means to make common, the opposite of holy (10:14-15).

decisions.choice: People of Israel, with "Men of Israel" as the alternative
decisions.reason: The inclusive default follows the meaning note; Literal keeps "men".

decisions.choice: God's law; this temple
decisions.reason: Readable says which law and which place.

source.text: ἦσαν γὰρ προεωρακότες Τρόφιμον τὸν Ἐφέσιον ἐν τῇ πόλει σὺν αὐτῷ, ὃν ἐνόμιζον ὅτι εἰς τὸ ἱερὸν εἰσήγαγεν ὁ Παῦλος.

records.literal_gloss: They were for having previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian in the city with him, whom they were supposing that into the temple brought Paul.

en.L: For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian in the city with him, whom they supposed that Paul had brought into the temple.
en.B: For they had seen Paul in the city a little earlier with Trophimus, a man of Ephesus, and they took it for granted that Paul had taken him into the temple.
en.R: They said this because they had seen Paul in the city with Trophimus, a Gentile from Ephesus. They thought Paul had taken him into the temple.

decisions.choice: Trophimus the Ephesian: a Gentile believer from Asia who traveled with Paul
decisions.reason: Trophimus was one of those who went with Paul (20:4). Paul later left him sick at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). As a Gentile he could not go beyond the outer court.

decisions.choice: they supposed: they assumed it, wrongly
decisions.reason: Luke uses this verb for a belief that turns out false (14:19, 16:27). He reports that they had seen Trophimus with Paul in the city, not in the temple.

decisions.choice: They said this because
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the link to the cry in 21:28.

decisions.choice: a Gentile from Ephesus
decisions.reason: Readable says why it mattered, as the meaning note explains.

source.text: ἐκινήθη τε ἡ πόλις ὅλη καὶ ἐγένετο συνδρομὴ τοῦ λαοῦ, καὶ ἐπιλαβόμενοι τοῦ Παύλου εἷλκον αὐτὸν ἔξω τοῦ ἱεροῦ, καὶ εὐθέως ἐκλείσθησαν αἱ θύραι.

records.literal_gloss: Was moved then the city whole and there was a running together of the people, and having seized Paul they were dragging him outside the temple, and immediately were shut the doors.

en.L: And the whole city was stirred, and there was a running together of the people, and having seized Paul, they dragged him outside the temple, and immediately the doors were shut.
en.B: The entire city was set in motion, and the people rushed together. They laid hold of Paul and hauled him out of the temple, and straightaway the gates were closed.
en.R: The whole city became upset, and people came running together. They grabbed Paul and dragged him out of the temple. Right away the temple gates were shut.

decisions.choice: the doors: the gates between the inner courts and the outer court
alternatives: the outer gates of the whole temple area
decisions.reason: Paul was dragged out of the inner courts into the outer court, and the temple guards (4:1) shut the gates behind him. The text does not say why; perhaps to keep the holy place from further defilement or from bloodshed.

decisions.choice: a running together: people rushing in from all sides
decisions.reason: The noun is used of a crowd running together.

decisions.choice: they were dragging him: the action is shown as it went on
decisions.reason: The imperfect pictures the scene as it happened.

decisions.choice: gates
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what kind of doors they were, as the meaning note explains.

source.text: ζητούντων τε αὐτὸν ἀποκτεῖναι ἀνέβη φάσις τῷ χιλιάρχῳ τῆς σπείρης ὅτι ὅλη συγχύννεται Ἰερουσαλήμ, ὃς ἐξαυτῆς παραλαβὼν στρατιώτας καὶ ἑκατοντάρχας κατέδραμεν ἐπ’ αὐτούς, οἱ δὲ ἰδόντες τὸν χιλίαρχον καὶ τοὺς στρατιώτας ἐπαύσαντο τύπτοντες τὸν Παῦλον.

records.literal_gloss: Seeking then [they] him to kill, went up a report to the tribune of the cohort that all is in confusion Jerusalem; \v 32 who at once having taken soldiers and centurions ran down upon them; they then having seen the tribune and the soldiers stopped beating Paul.

en.L: And while they were seeking to kill him, a report went up to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. \v 32 He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down upon them, and when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
en.B: They were set on killing him when a report went up to the tribune in command of the cohort that the whole of Jerusalem was in turmoil. \v 32 He immediately took soldiers and centurions and rushed down on the crowd, and at the sight of the tribune and the soldiers they left off beating Paul.
en.R: They were trying to kill Paul. Then someone told the tribune, the commander of the Roman soldiers in Jerusalem, that the whole city was in an uproar. \v 32 Right away the tribune took soldiers and their officers, called centurions, and ran down to the crowd. When the people saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped hitting Paul.

decisions.choice: the tribune of the cohort: the Roman officer commanding the troops in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: A tribune was a Roman officer; the title means commander of a thousand. A cohort was a unit of several hundred soldiers. This cohort was kept in the Antonia fortress beside the temple. The tribune's name was Claudius Lysias (23:26).

decisions.choice: went up; ran down: the fortress stood above the temple courts
decisions.reason: Josephus says the Antonia fortress overlooked the temple from the northwest, with stairs down to the colonnades, and that soldiers watched the crowds there at the feasts (Jewish War 5.238-247).

decisions.choice: centurions: officers over about a hundred soldiers each
decisions.reason: The plural shows the tribune took a large force, perhaps two hundred men or more.

decisions.choice: they stopped beating Paul: the crowd had been beating him
alternatives: they did not start to beat him
decisions.reason: The verb means to stop doing something already under way.

decisions.choice: the commander of the Roman soldiers in Jerusalem; their officers, called centurions
alternatives: the tribune of the cohort; centurions
decisions.reason: Readable says who the tribune and the centurions were, as the meaning notes explain.

decisions.choice: the tribune in command of the cohort
decisions.reason: Balanced says how the tribune was related to the cohort.

source.text: τότε ἐγγίσας ὁ χιλίαρχος ἐπελάβετο αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐκέλευσε δεθῆναι ἁλύσεσι δυσί, καὶ ἐπυνθάνετο τίς εἴη καὶ τί ἐστιν πεποιηκώς.

records.literal_gloss: Then having drawn near the tribune seized him and ordered [him] to be bound with chains two, and was inquiring who he might be and what he has been doing.

en.L: Then the tribune came near, seized him, and ordered [him] to be bound with two chains, and he inquired who he might be and what he had done.
en.B: Coming up to Paul, the tribune took him into custody and gave orders to fasten him with two chains. He began asking who the man was and what he had been doing.
en.R: The tribune came over and arrested Paul. He told his soldiers to put two chains on him. Then he asked the people who this man was and what he had done.

decisions.choice: two chains: Paul was most likely chained to a soldier on each side
decisions.reason: Peter was held the same way, between two soldiers with two chains (12:6).

decisions.choice: bound: Agabus's word begins to come true
decisions.reason: Agabus said Paul would be bound in Jerusalem and handed over to the Gentiles (21:11). Now a Roman officer binds him.

decisions.choice: he inquired: he asked the crowd, not Paul
decisions.reason: The answers come from the crowd (21:34). The question "who he might be" shows he did not know whom he had arrested.

decisions.choice: asked the people
decisions.reason: Readable names whom he asked, as the meaning note explains.

source.text: ἄλλοι δὲ ἄλλο τι ἐπεφώνουν ἐν τῷ ὄχλῳ· μὴ δυναμένου δὲ αὐτοῦ γνῶναι τὸ ἀσφαλὲς διὰ τὸν θόρυβον ἐκέλευσεν ἄγεσθαι αὐτὸν εἰς τὴν παρεμβολήν.

records.literal_gloss: Others however something other were shouting in the crowd; not being able then he to know the certain [thing] because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks.

en.L: But some in the crowd were shouting one thing, others another, and since he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks.
en.B: But the crowd shouted back, some one thing, some another. The din made it impossible for him to get at the facts, so he had Paul taken into the barracks.
en.R: Some people in the crowd shouted one thing, and others shouted something else. There was so much noise that the tribune could not find out what had really happened. So he ordered his soldiers to take Paul into the fortress where they lived.

decisions.choice: the barracks: the soldiers' quarters in the Antonia fortress
decisions.reason: The word means a camp or barracks. Here it is the quarters of the cohort in the fortress beside the temple (21:31).

decisions.choice: the facts: what was certain
decisions.reason: The word means what is firm or certain, as in 22:30 and 25:26.

decisions.choice: some shouted one thing, some another: a crowd in confusion
decisions.reason: Luke describes the town assembly at Ephesus the same way (19:32).

decisions.choice: the fortress where they lived
decisions.reason: Readable says what the barracks were, as the meaning note explains.

source.text: ὅτε δὲ ἐγένετο ἐπὶ τοὺς ἀναβαθμούς, συνέβη βαστάζεσθαι αὐτὸν ὑπὸ τῶν στρατιωτῶν διὰ τὴν βίαν τοῦ ὄχλου, ἠκολούθει γὰρ τὸ πλῆθος τοῦ λαοῦ κράζοντες· Αἶρε αὐτόν.

records.literal_gloss: When now he came upon the stairs, it happened [that] to be carried he by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd; \v 36 were following for the multitude of the people, crying out, Away with him!

en.L: And when he came to the stairs, it happened that he was carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd, \v 36 for the multitude of the people kept following, crying out, "Away with him!"
en.B: At the stairs, the crowd's violence was such that the soldiers had to carry Paul up. \v 36 The whole mass of people came after them, crying out, "Away with him!"
en.R: When they came to the steps of the fortress, the crowd was so wild that the soldiers had to carry Paul. \v 36 The whole crowd followed them and kept shouting, "Kill him!"

decisions.choice: the stairs: the steps from the temple's outer court up to the fortress
alternatives: the steps of the inner courts
decisions.reason: Josephus says stairs led down from the Antonia to the colonnades of the temple (Jewish War 5.243).

decisions.choice: Away with him: the cry raised against Jesus
decisions.reason: The crowd cried the same words before Pilate (Luke 23:18; John 19:15). In 22:22 they add that such a man should not be allowed to live, so it is a call for his death.

decisions.choice: for: the crowd pressing after them explains why Paul was carried
decisions.reason: The word "for" ties the following crowd to the violence in 21:35.

decisions.choice: Kill him!
decisions.reason: Readable says what the cry meant, as the meaning note explains.

source.text: Μέλλων τε εἰσάγεσθαι εἰς τὴν παρεμβολὴν ὁ Παῦλος λέγει τῷ χιλιάρχῳ· Εἰ ἔξεστίν μοι εἰπεῖν τι πρὸς σέ;

records.literal_gloss: Being about then to be brought into the barracks Paul says to the tribune, If it is permitted to me to say something to you?

en.L: And as he was about to be brought into the barracks, Paul says to the tribune, "Is it permitted for me to say something to you?"
en.B: As they were about to take him into the barracks, Paul said to the tribune, "May I have a word with you?"
en.R: The soldiers were about to take Paul into the fortress. Then Paul said to the tribune, "Please, may I speak with you?"

decisions.choice: a direct question, opened with the word for "if"
alternatives: "if I may say something", an unfinished sentence
decisions.reason: Greek of the time could open a direct question this way (1:6, 19:2).

decisions.choice: says: a present tense in a past story
decisions.reason: Luke uses the present to make the scene vivid; the event itself is past.

decisions.choice: Paul asks in Greek, the common language of the eastern empire
decisions.reason: The tribune's surprise in 21:37-38 shows that Paul spoke to him in Greek.

decisions.choice: said
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the past tense, as the meaning note explains.

source.text: ὁ δὲ ἔφη· Ἑλληνιστὶ γινώσκεις;

records.literal_gloss: He then was saying, Greek do you know?

en.L: And he said, "Do you know Greek?
en.B: The tribune said, "You know Greek?
en.R: The tribune said, "You can speak Greek?

decisions.choice: Greek: the Greek language
decisions.reason: The adverb means "in Greek"; with "know" it means knowing the language.

decisions.choice: the tribune's surprise
decisions.reason: He had taken Paul for a rebel from Egypt (21:38) and did not expect him to speak educated Greek.

decisions.choice: The tribune
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speaker.

source.text: οὐκ ἄρα σὺ εἶ ὁ Αἰγύπτιος ὁ πρὸ τούτων τῶν ἡμερῶν ἀναστατώσας καὶ ἐξαγαγὼν εἰς τὴν ἔρημον τοὺς τετρακισχιλίους ἄνδρας τῶν σικαρίων;

records.literal_gloss: Not then you are the Egyptian, the [one] before these the days having stirred up a revolt and having led out into the wilderness the four thousand men of the Sicarii?

en.L: Then are you not the Egyptian who before these days stirred up a revolt and led out into the wilderness the 4,000 men of the Sicarii?"
en.B: So you are not the Egyptian who stirred up a rebellion a while ago and led the 4,000 men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?"
en.R: I thought you were the Egyptian who started a rebellion some time ago. He led 4,000 armed men called Assassins out into the desert."

decisions.choice: So you are not the Egyptian: the tribune realizes he was mistaken
alternatives: "Are you not the Egyptian?", expecting the answer yes
decisions.reason: The two opening words usually mark surprise at something just learned: a man who speaks Greek like this is not who he thought. Others read the question as expecting Paul to say he is the Egyptian.

decisions.choice: the Egyptian: a rebel known from Josephus
decisions.reason: Josephus tells of an Egyptian false prophet in the time of Felix who gathered followers in the wilderness and led them to the Mount of Olives, saying Jerusalem's walls would fall at his command. Felix's troops scattered them and the Egyptian escaped (Jewish War 2.261-263; Antiquities 20.169-172). Josephus gives larger numbers, and his two accounts differ.

decisions.choice: the Sicarii: the "dagger men", a group of assassins
decisions.reason: The word is borrowed from Latin and means men with daggers. Josephus says that under Felix they killed opponents in the festival crowds in Jerusalem with short daggers hidden in their clothes (Jewish War 2.254-257). Luke links the Egyptian's followers with them; Josephus describes the two separately.

decisions.choice: the wilderness: the desert country
decisions.reason: The word means empty, uninhabited land, like the wilderness of Judea.

decisions.choice: the Sicarii
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the borrowed Latin word, as the Greek does.

decisions.choice: Assassins
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable translate the name; "Assassins" says what they did without a modern label.

decisions.choice: a statement: I thought you were the Egyptian
decisions.reason: Readable states what the question implies, as the first meaning note explains.

source.text: εἶπεν δὲ ὁ Παῦλος· Ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπος μέν εἰμι Ἰουδαῖος, Ταρσεὺς τῆς Κιλικίας, οὐκ ἀσήμου πόλεως πολίτης· δέομαι δέ σου, ἐπίτρεψόν μοι λαλῆσαι πρὸς τὸν λαόν.

records.literal_gloss: Said however Paul, I a man indeed am a Jew, of Tarsus of Cilicia, not of an insignificant city a citizen; I beg now you, allow me to speak to the people.

en.L: But Paul said, "I am a Jewish man, of Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. And I beg you, allow me to speak to the people."
en.B: Paul answered, "I am a Jew, a man of Tarsus in Cilicia, and a citizen of a city of some note. I ask you, allow me to address the people."
en.R: Paul answered, "No, I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia. Tarsus is an important city, and I am a citizen there. Please let me speak to the people."

decisions.choice: I am a Jew ... now I ask: the first part answers the question, the second makes a request
decisions.reason: The paired particles set Paul's answer, that he is a Jew and not the Egyptian, beside his request.

decisions.choice: Tarsus: the chief city of Cilicia, known for its schools
decisions.reason: Tarsus lay in the southeast of what is now Turkey. "No insignificant city" is understatement for a city of some fame. Paul was born there (9:11, 22:3).

decisions.choice: citizen: a citizen of Tarsus
decisions.reason: Paul speaks here of his city. That he is also a Roman citizen comes out in 22:25-28.

decisions.choice: the people: the Jewish crowd
decisions.reason: Luke uses this word for the people of Israel (21:28, 21:30, 21:36).

decisions.choice: a city of some note
decisions.reason: Balanced states the understatement plainly, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: No
decisions.reason: Readable makes plain that Paul's answer denies being the Egyptian, as the first meaning note explains.

source.text: ἐπιτρέψαντος δὲ αὐτοῦ ὁ Παῦλος ἑστὼς ἐπὶ τῶν ἀναβαθμῶν κατέσεισε τῇ χειρὶ τῷ λαῷ, πολλῆς δὲ σιγῆς γενομένης προσεφώνησεν τῇ Ἑβραΐδι διαλέκτῳ λέγων

records.literal_gloss: Having allowed [him] then he, Paul having stood on the stairs motioned with the hand to the people; great then silence having come, he addressed [them] in the Hebrew language, saying,

en.L: And when he had given permission, Paul, standing on the stairs, motioned with [his] hand to the people, and when a great silence had come, he addressed [them] in the Hebrew dialect, saying:
en.B: The tribune gave permission, and Paul, standing on the steps, raised his hand to the people. When all had fallen silent, he spoke to them in the Hebrew language. He said:
en.R: The tribune said he could. So Paul stood on the steps and raised his hand to get the people's attention. They all became very quiet. Then Paul spoke to them in the Jews' own language. He said:

decisions.choice: saying: the sentence runs on into Paul's speech, which begins at 22:1
decisions.reason: The chapter break falls between "saying" and the words Paul spoke, so this record ends with the speech still to come.

decisions.choice: the Hebrew language: the language of the Jews of the land, most likely Aramaic
alternatives: Hebrew, the language of the Scriptures
decisions.reason: Greek writers of the time used "Hebrew" both for Hebrew and for Aramaic, the everyday language of the Jews in Judea. John calls Aramaic place names "Hebrew" (John 19:13, 19:17). Paul could have used either, and the text does not settle it.

decisions.choice: motioning with the hand: a gesture asking for silence
decisions.reason: Peter and Paul make the same gesture before speaking (12:17, 13:16).

decisions.choice: speaking the people's own language won a hearing
decisions.reason: When they hear him speak in it, they grow even quieter (22:2).

decisions.choice: The tribune
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name who gave permission.

decisions.choice: the Jews' own language
decisions.reason: Readable names the language by whose it was, which keeps open whether it was Hebrew or Aramaic, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: dialect; language
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Greek word; Balanced says language, which is what it means here.
